label: Problem set 9
title: Problem set 9: Hydrodynamic methods
summary: Practice with the rotating disk electrode: the Levich equation, mass-transfer coefficients, rotation-rate dependence and Koutecky-Levich analysis.

intro.text: The rotating disk electrode gives a steady-state, mass-transfer-limited current described by the Levich equation iL = 0.62 n F A D^(2/3) omega^(1/2) nu^(-1/6) C, with omega = 2 pi f.
Because iL is proportional to omega^(1/2), a Koutecky-Levich plot of 1/i against 1/omega^(1/2) separates mass transfer from kinetics, giving the kinetic current as the intercept.

blocks.text: The rotating disk electrode gives a steady-state, mass-transfer-limited current described by the Levich equation iL = 0.62 n F A D^(2/3) omega^(1/2) nu^(-1/6) C, with omega = 2 pi f.
Because iL is proportional to omega^(1/2), a Koutecky-Levich plot of 1/i against 1/omega^(1/2) separates mass transfer from kinetics, giving the kinetic current as the intercept.

blocks.title: Levich limiting current
steps: Use iL = 0.62 n F A D^(2/3) omega^(1/2) nu^(-1/6) C.

questions.question: Use the Levich equation iL = 0.62 n F A D^(2/3) omega^(1/2) nu^(-1/6) C for n = 1, A = 0.30 cm2, D = 1.0e-5 cm2/s, rotation frequency 10 r/s (omega = 2 pi f = 62.8 s-1), nu = 0.010 cm2/s, C = 1.0e-5 mol/cm3. Calculate iL in mA.
The Levich limiting current is proportional to omega^(1/2). If the rotation rate is quadrupled, by what factor does iL change?
questions.explanation: iL scales with sqrt(omega), so quadrupling the rotation rate multiplies iL by sqrt(4) = 2.0.

questions.question: Calculate the mass-transfer coefficient m = 0.62 D^(2/3) omega^(1/2) nu^(-1/6) in cm/s for D = 1.0e-5 cm2/s, omega = 62.8 s-1 and nu = 0.010 cm2/s.
The rotating disk electrode is widely used because it:
options: Gives a steady-state, reproducible and uniformly accessible mass-transfer rate
questions.explanation: The RDE gives a well-defined, steady-state, uniform flux to the disk, so its limiting current is given by the Levich equation and is easy to model.

questions.question: The Koutecky-Levich analysis separates the mass-transfer-limited current from the kinetic current.
questions.explanation: Plotting 1/i against 1/omega^(1/2) gives a line whose intercept is 1/ik and whose slope contains the mass-transfer term, so both the kinetic current and the rate constant can be extracted.

questions.question: In a Koutecky-Levich plot of 1/i against 1/omega^(1/2), the intercept equals:
options: 1/ik, the reciprocal of the kinetic current
questions.explanation: As the rotation rate becomes very large, mass transfer stops limiting and the current approaches the kinetic current ik; the extrapolated intercept is 1/ik.

questions.question: At a rotation rate where the mass-transfer-limited current would be 2.0 mA, a reaction still has a finite kinetic current of 2.0 mA. Using 1/i = 1/ik + 1/iL, calculate the measured current in mA.
questions.explanation: 1/i = 1/2.0 + 1/2.0 = 1.0, so i = 1.0 mA. When kinetics and mass transfer are comparable, the measured current is lower than either alone.

questions.question: The Levich equation applies to a rotating disk electrode under fully mass-transfer-limited conditions.
questions.explanation: Under the limiting condition the surface concentration is zero and the Levich equation gives the steady-state limiting current as a function of rotation rate and diffusion coefficient.

questions.question: Which are features of the rotating disk electrode? Select all that apply.
options: Uniform accessibility of the disk surface
questions.explanation: The RDE reaches a steady state, the surface is uniformly accessible, and the limiting current follows Levich, proportional to omega^(1/2). The t^(-1/2) decay belongs to diffusion to a still planar electrode.

questions.question: The Levich current is proportional to omega^(1/2). If iL = 1.42 mA at 10 r/s, what is iL in mA at 40 r/s?
questions.explanation: omega increases by 4, so sqrt(omega) and iL increase by 2: iL = 2 x 1.42 = 2.84 mA.

questions.question: Use the Levich equation iL = 0.62 nFAD^(2/3)omega^(1/2)nu^(-1/6)C, proportional to concentration. If iL = 1.42 mA at C = 1.0e-5 mol/cm3, what is iL in mA at C = 2.0e-5 mol/cm3?
questions.explanation: The Levich current is proportional to C, so doubling C doubles iL to 2.84 mA.

questions.question: The rotating disk electrode surface is described as uniformly accessible because:
options: Every point on the disk experiences the same mass-transfer rate
The edge reacts ten times faster
questions.explanation: The hydrodynamic flow gives the same flux to every point of the disk, so the current distribution is uniform - a key reason the RDE is so reproducible.

questions.question: The mass-transfer coefficient at an RDE depends on the rotation rate but not on the concentration.
questions.explanation: The mass-transfer coefficient m = 0.62 D^(2/3) omega^(1/2) nu^(-1/6) contains D, omega and nu but no concentration, so it is independent of C.

questions.question: Which are applications of the rotating disk electrode? Select all that apply.
options: Measuring electrode kinetics by Koutecky-Levich analysis
Studying electrocatalysts under defined mass transport
Measuring the pH of the solution directly
questions.explanation: The RDE is used for kinetics, catalysis and diffusion measurements under well-defined transport. It does not measure pH directly.
